messages.author: 23246b06cdd7e17b
messages.subject: AKDE for a herd
parts:
Hi Chris,

I am starting an RSF analysis for my bison herds and would like to define the extent of area used by multiple individuals within a single herd. I would like to use AKDE instead of the traditional MCP. Will the 'overlap' tool help me to define the area used by all the individuals (which I already calculated AKDE for) or should I recalculate AKDE using all the GPS points together? I was wondering what you would recommend. Thanks in advance for your help!

Sincerely,

Robert Ritson

messages.author: 40fd627580dd34f5
messages.subject: Re: AKDE for a herd
parts:
Hi Robert,

I would avoid that route and instead try to add spatially constraining terms to the model, as is done in "synoptic" home-range estimation. This effectively adds a smooth notion of availability (really, it is site fidelity now) that is fit to the data simultaneously with the covariate dependence, instead of a (typically) discontinuous spatial constraint that is chosen a priori. Also, fitting the spatial dependence first, as is typically done with MCP->RSF, doesn't allow the model to completely tease apart the two influences, and so robs the covariates of some of their explanatory power.

Just make sure your data satisfies the IID assumptions when doing RSFs. If you need to thin the data but want to use all of the data, then you can run all possible coarsenings of the data and average the results together (without shrinking the standard errors).

Best,
Chris

messages.author: 961f4ec0bd606336
messages.subject: Re: AKDE for a herd
parts:
Hi Chris (& Robert),

The method you mention for adding a spatially constraining term sounds interesting. I have a similar problem--I'm running RSFs for birds that are central-place foragers, so they are constrained by distance to the nest (although they can still fly shockingly far). Right now I'm running an RSF model that includes a "distance to nest" parameter. Is this what you mean by adding spatially constraining term to the model?

I'm not sure how this concept can be used in the generation of "available" environment. As I understand, the available environment is usually based on some a priori defined extent, often the animal's home range. I think this is what Robert was describing in his question. Then, you generate a bunch of random points (or, if using a point process, a grid of points), within the area that you've defined as the available extent to define the available environment. How is it possible to avoid this step using the method you described?

Is there perhaps a paper with an example of how to do this? I think that would be really helpful!

Thank you,

Ben

messages.author: 40fd627580dd34f5
messages.subject: Re: AKDE for a herd
parts:
Hi Ben,

"distance to nest" is one possibility, though you might want to try different powers. E.g., square distance to nest gives you a Gaussian in the absence of covariates.
Hi Ben,

There are different ways to integrate the RSFs/SSFs. One way is to sample uniformly over the "available" region, but this necessarily presumes a finite "available" region, which is a model choice.
A better way is to sample with a pilot density, if you have one. Say your RSF depends on square distance to nest, like this

RSF(x) = exp(-(x-nest)^2/(2 Sigma))/(2 pi Sigma) exp(-beta*covariates(x)) / Normalization

where nest, Sigma, beta are the parameters of your model and

Normalization = integral exp(-(x-nest)^2/(2 Sigma))/(2 pi Sigma) exp(-beta*covariates(x)) dx

but note that this is the same as the expectation value

< exp(-beta*covariates(x)) >_p

with respect to the pilot density

p(x) = exp(-(x-nest)^2/(2 Sigma))/(2 pi Sigma)

The "available" region can now formally extend to infinity without divergence, but when drawing random locations from p(x) you tend to sample a concentrated region around the nest.

As for references to people that do this, I would try the "synoptic home range" literature, but I don't really recall their numerics. I know I've seen this kind of trick used with in SSFs, but there its mostly for fitting the step & resource parameters simultaneously. The first paper I know of that did something like that was Avgar's integrated SSF paper.

There really should be a canonical reference on different methods to perform the RSF/SSF integration. Most RSF/SSF papers don't even explain that the random sampling is a Monte-Carlo approximation to the normalization integral.

Best,
Chris
